newsitem.title: UK: OPEC output continues upward creep, mkt takes it.
newsitem.headline: OPEC output continues upward creep, mkt takes it.

text.p: OPEC oil output continued its upward climb in November and analysts see no reason for the trend to change in coming months even though Iraq's long-delayed return to world oil markets appears imminent.

A Reuter survey of oil analysts, industry sources and OPEC delegates on Thursday showed that the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries pumped out 26.08 million barrels per day (bpd), up from 25.97 million in October.

It marked the first time OPEC daily output has topped 26 million since 1980 when the group had 13 members, two more than now. That figure does not even include the full 1.2 million bpd Iraq is expected to pump when the United Nations oil sale plan is implemented in the next few weeks.
"Our base case is for an upward creep into next year and that is even without the Iraqi oil," said Leo Drollas, chief economist at the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES).

But Drollas and other oil analysts stop short of predicting a collapse in the oil price before mid-1997 given buoyant demand, low heating oil stocks and the possibility of a repeat of last winter's deep freeze.
"The market has taken every barrel of OPEC oil this year and will continue taking at least until the second quarter next year," said Geoff Pyne, energy economist at Swiss bank UBS.

While the demand surge and setbacks in output gains from producers outside OPEC has worked in OPEC's favour this year, bringing it an extra $30 billion in oil revenue, a glut could result once peak winter demand subsides, analysts say.
Pyne reckons daily OPEC output will rise some 850,000-900,000 barrels in 1997 if Iraq returns to the market.
"On paper the numbers work against OPEC. I figure OPEC output this time next year will be over 27 million and demand (for OPEC oil) will only be around 26.3 million," Pyne said.
Drollas is more bearish, predicting a sharp price fall and "tremendous loss" in OPEC oil revenue because of higher global oil supplies and a slowdown in demand.
"The market will take a hammering in the second half if you have an extra 600,000 barrels a day of Iraqi oil and no OPEC cuts," Drollas said.

The surprisingly resilient oil price, now about $5 over 1995 levels, has tempted most of OPEC to exceed individual quotas, pushing collective production more than one million bpd over its 25.03 million ceiling.
Last week, OPEC ministers meeting in Vienna decided to freeze that ceiling until at least late June when they meet again.

The growing prospect that about 500,000-600,000 bpd of Iraqi oil could hit the market by the end of the year now that most of the obstacles blocking a $2 billion U.N. oil-for-food deal are gone sealed the OPEC freeze and returned the spotlight on quota violations.
In November, Venezuela continued as OPEC's biggest quota buster, pumping 3.15 million a day, well over its 2.36 million quota.

Despite repeated public denials by Oil Minister Erwin Arrieta at last week's talks, most OPEC members believe the South American country is over quota and Venezuelan oil industry officials privately confirm this.
"The other ministers really bent his (Arrieta's) ear in Vienna last week about the cheating but he became emotional and refused to admit to anything," an OPEC official said.
Iran's Oil Minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh, head of OPEC's quota compliance committee, said Arrieta refused to admit "even one barrel of overproduction."
"There is no way Venezuela will ever look back now. For all practical purposes, it is not really a member of OPEC now," said Mohammed Abduljabbar, an oil consultant at Petroleum Finance Corp (PFC).

The three powerful Middle East Gulf members, Saudi Arabia, UAE and Kuwait, have remained relatively restrained considering they are the only countries in the world with serious spare oil production capacity, OPEC delegates say.
But all three were slightly over quota in November though Saudi Arabia said its market supply, which is how OPEC determines quotas, remains at quota of eight million.

"If they (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE) would unleash their unused capacity, it could devastate this market. But at the moment they choose to play price not politics so they are resisting the temptation to pump it out," said Bo Van Wijk, vice president energy risk management at UBS in Zurich.
The Reuter survey saw Saudi wellhead production up slightly at 8.15 million bpd from 8.05 in October. It also saw higher output from Algeria, Iran, Libya and Qatar.
The Reuter survey seeks a best estimate of wellhead flows in OPEC countries based on the views of officials, industry monitors and analysts inside and outside member countries.
OPEC quotas are based on supply to market, defined to exclude movements to, but not sales from storage.
